title: Symphony No. 6 in A minor, “Tragic”
hook: The symphony in which Mahler brings a hammer onto the stage.

painting.title: The Woodcutter
painting.pairingNote: A man swings his axe at a tree, the image Mahler himself used for the hammer blows (“like the fall of an axe”), painted by a Swiss contemporary.

facts: Mahler wrote the symphony in the summers of 1903 and 1904 at Maiernigg, his lakeside retreat on the Wörthersee in southern Austria, and kept revising it until 1906. He conducted the premiere in Essen on 27 May 1906.

These were happy years: he had married Alma Schindler in 1902, and their second daughter was born in June 1904. Yet this is his darkest symphony, and the only one of his symphonies that ends in the minor.
The nickname “Tragic” is not in the score. Bruno Walter wrote that Mahler called it his “Tragic Symphony”, and the programme of the first Vienna performance, in January 1907, printed “Tragische”.

The order of the middle movements is still argued over. Mahler composed and published the work with the Scherzo second. During the rehearsals for the premiere he moved the Andante to second place, and he kept that order in the three performances he conducted. In 1919 Alma Mahler sent the conductor Willem Mengelberg a telegram saying “first Scherzo, then Andante”, and the critical edition of 1963 followed her; later research has argued for Andante first again. Conductors still choose either. This recording plays the Scherzo second.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a march fought to a bright end (I), the same march twisted into a grotesque dance (II), a song from far away (III), a half-hour battle that ends in defeat (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro energico, ma non troppo
movements.title: Allegro energico, ma non troppo
movements.summary: A relentless march in A minor, *heftig, aber markig* (vehement but sturdy). Against it Mahler sets a soaring melody that Alma said was a portrait of her. The movement is a classical [[sonata-form|sonata form]], with its whole first part repeated, and it ends in a blaze of A major: the brightest moment of the symphony.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: basses and cellos tramp out a rhythm, then the violins leap and stride in wide, angry intervals.
The [[motto|motto]]: trumpets play a loud major chord that drains into a soft minor one, over a fixed drum rhythm on the timpani. It comes back in every movement.

mainIdeas.name: The “Alma theme”
mainIdeas.description: a long, sweeping violin melody that surges upward, warm and impatient.

stops.hear: Low strings march on one note with a snare drum; the violins break in with a fierce, leaping tune
stops.happening: The main theme. The whole movement is built on this march

stops.hear: The trumpets blare a major chord, which fades into minor as the oboes take over; under it the timpani beat a stiff rhythm
stops.happening: The motto, the symphony’s signature. Happiness turning into its opposite in a few seconds

stops.hear: Quiet woodwind chords like a slow hymn, with strings plucking softly
stops.happening: A [[chorale|chorale]] that links the two main themes

stops.hear: The violins sweep upward in a passionate melody
stops.happening: The “Alma theme”, the second theme

stops.hear: The march starts again from the beginning
stops.happening: Mahler asks for the whole [[exposition|exposition]] to be repeated, something he did in only one other symphony

stops.hear: The march returns, harsher, broken into pieces and driven through strange keys
stops.happening: The [[development|development]]

stops.hear: The march stops. Distant cowbells tinkle, a celesta glitters, high strings hold still
stops.happening: A vision of high mountain pastures, far from the struggle. The [[cowbells|cowbells]] are played [[offstage|offstage]]

stops.hear: A jolt, and the march is back at full speed
stops.happening: The idyll is over

stops.hear: The opening march theme returns in A minor
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]]

stops.hear: The music slows down and turns warm and yearning
stops.happening: Currentzis lingers over the calmer themes as they return

stops.hear: The “Alma theme” returns in A major at full power, and the movement races to a bright, hammered close
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]]. The last major-key ending in the symphony

notice: Listen to the motto at about 1:40. The same chord changes from major to minor while the drum rhythm stays the same. When it returns later in the symphony, it marks a turning point.
Compare the cowbell episode with the march around it. Mahler wanted the bells to sound like a herd grazing in the distance, a world the march cannot reach.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Currentzis takes the repeat of the exposition, which is why the movement lasts almost 25 minutes. He slows down a great deal in the quiet passages and drives hard in the loud ones, and he starts the Scherzo almost without a pause.

movements.heading: Scherzo
movements.title: Scherzo: Wuchtig
movements.summary: The march comes back, but now in three beats instead of four, heavy and lurching: Mahler marks it *Wuchtig*, “weighty”. Twice it gives way to a dainty, old-fashioned dance that keeps tripping over its own feet. The movement is a distorted mirror of the first.

mainIdeas.description: The [[scherzo|scherzo]]: stamping low strings and timpani, shrill woodwinds, yelping horns, the clatter of the xylophone.
The [[trio|trio]]: marked *Altväterisch* (“old-fashioned”), a polite little dance in the woodwinds in which the number of beats in the bar keeps changing.

stops.hear: Heavy, stamping chords in the low strings and timpani
stops.happening: The first movement’s march rhythm, squeezed into triple time

stops.hear: Shrieking woodwinds, honking horns, a rattling xylophone
stops.happening: The dance turns grotesque, almost a caricature

stops.hear: The tempo eases; the woodwinds lead a delicate, limping dance
stops.happening: The [[trio|trio]]. It sounds like an old minuet that cannot keep its balance, because the metre keeps switching

stops.hear: The stamping returns
stops.happening: The scherzo again, more violent

stops.hear: The old-fashioned dance comes back, in new colours
stops.happening: The second trio

stops.hear: The weighty dance once more
stops.happening: The last return of the scherzo

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music runs down into fragments: a woodwind sigh, a few low notes, quiet drum taps
stops.happening: The movement dies away instead of ending

notice: Tap the rhythm of the opening and compare it with the first movement’s march. The pattern is the same, but with three beats instead of four it limps.

Alma Mahler wrote that this movement pictured their two small daughters “tottering in zigzags over the sand”. The dates do not fit: when Mahler wrote the movement in 1903, his first daughter was less than a year old and the second not yet born.

movements.heading: Andante moderato
movements.title: Andante moderato
movements.summary: The only movement that is not haunted by the march. In E-flat major, far from A minor, a gentle song unfolds in the strings and woodwinds. Cowbells sound again, now inside the orchestra, and the music grows to a broad, glowing climax before settling into calm.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a tender, introspective phrase for the violins, which often clouds over towards the minor.

mainIdeas.name: The woodwind songs
mainIdeas.description: plaintive solos for the woodwinds and horn that answer the strings.

stops.hear: The violins sing a quiet, tender melody
stops.happening: The main theme, in E-flat major

stops.hear: A sadder, wandering melody in the woodwinds
stops.happening: The second idea, leaning towards the minor

stops.hear: The opening melody returns, with the horn joining in
stops.happening: The main theme for the second time

stops.hear: Cowbells tinkle softly within the orchestra; the music drifts to a distant key
stops.happening: The mountain pastures return, closer now

stops.hear: The violins take up the main theme again, warmer and fuller
stops.happening: Its third appearance

stops.hear: The strings slide from note to note on swelling phrases
stops.happening: Mahler’s [[glissando|glissando]] markings, which Currentzis lets you hear

stops.hear: The full orchestra opens out, horns blazing, cowbells clashing
stops.happening: The climax of the movement

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: The storm passes; quiet woodwinds and strings, a long, soft E-flat chord
stops.happening: Calm returns

notice: Listen to the end of each phrase of the main theme. It often slips into the minor for a moment before finding its way back.

movements.heading: Finale
movements.title: Finale: Sostenuto – Allegro moderato – Allegro energico
movements.summary: More than half an hour long, the battle of the whole symphony. A dark, slow introduction leads to a march that keeps fighting its way upward and is struck down by two blows of a [[hammer|hammer]]. Mahler’s instruction for the sound: “brief and mighty, but dull in resonance and with a non-metallic character (like the fall of an axe)”. The end is in A minor, without the major chord.

mainIdeas.name: The introduction
mainIdeas.description: a shimmering swirl in the high strings, harps and celesta, a violin phrase that climbs and then sinks, dark chords in the brass and tuba.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: a fierce main theme in A minor, led by the horns and strings.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: a bright, leaping tune that seems to promise victory.

mainIdeas.name: The motto
mainIdeas.description: the major-to-minor chord from the first movement, which returns at turning points.

stops.hear: A sudden, shimmering swirl of sound in the high strings and celesta; a violin melody climbs and falls back
stops.happening: The introduction, *Sostenuto*

stops.hear: A major chord in the brass collapses into minor over the timpani rhythm
stops.happening: The [[motto|motto]] again, at the very start of the battle

stops.hear: A slow, dark landscape: deep brass, tuba, horn calls, scraps of a hymn
stops.happening: The introduction gathers the ideas of the whole movement

stops.hear: The tempo picks up and a fierce march begins
stops.happening: The *Allegro*. The main theme, in A minor

stops.hear: A brighter, leaping theme in the horns and violins
stops.happening: The second theme. For a moment, victory seems possible

stops.hear: The march breaks off; the shimmer of the introduction returns, then distant cowbells and a dreamy pause
stops.happening: The [[development|development]] opens with a memory of the mountains

stops.hear: The march gathers to a huge climax, crowned by a heavy, dull crash
stops.happening: The first hammer blow. The music races on

stops.hear: Another climax, and the second dull crash
stops.happening: The second hammer blow. This time the music seethes and struggles on

stops.hear: The shimmering swirl and dark brass of the opening
stops.happening: The introduction returns, as at the beginning

stops.hear: The march resumes
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]]. The themes come back, in a new order

stops.hear: A last upheaval that breaks off into stillness
stops.happening: Here a third hammer blow fell in the first printed score. Mahler removed it, and Currentzis follows him

stops.hear: Very quiet, very low: trombones and tuba play a slow lament
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]]. For a few bars they seem to offer comfort, then fade

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A sudden, shattering chord in A minor, with the drum rhythm of the motto, then silence
stops.happening: The motto without its major chord. The end

notice: Count the hammer blows. Alma Mahler said her husband described them as three blows of fate falling on a hero, “the third of which fells him like a tree”. Mahler cut the third, and the passage where it was now ends in a sudden stillness.
Listen to the very last chord. In the first movement, the motto always went from major to minor. Here there is no major chord left.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Currentzis uses two hammer blows, as in Mahler’s revision. Reviewers noted that he does not make them deafening: what matters to him is what happens after each one, a sudden acceleration after the first and a seething struggle after the second.

threads.title: Major turning into minor
threads.body: The motto chord sums up the symphony: a moment of light that drains into darkness. The first movement still ends in A major; the finale ends on the minor chord alone.

threads.title: The march
threads.body: The first movement’s march returns in triple time in the Scherzo and fights its last battle in the finale. Only the Andante escapes it.

threads.title: Cowbells
threads.body: In the first movement, the Andante and the finale, the bells open a door to a distant, peaceful world. Each time, the struggle closes it again.

threads.title: Two orders
threads.body: Played with the Scherzo second, as here, the march rhythm hammers through the first half of the symphony and the Andante comes as a release before the finale. With the Andante second, the Scherzo leads straight into the finale’s darkness. Abbado’s recording, listed below, uses that order.
